intro: Eindhoven's old trees are mostly Philips trees. A horse chestnut planted in 1909 because the company believed staff worked better with something green to look at, now at gate 11 of the stadium. An oak in twenty five hectares Anton Philips gave to the city in 1920. A sequoia in the pinetum on the estate his son lived on until 2005, shut for a century and opened in September 2025. The two that owe Philips nothing are the oldest and the best loved: a beech from before the industrial town, and an oak the neighbours light every December.
meta_description: Sixteen remarkable trees in Eindhoven: the 1909 Philips chestnut, a plane set on fire and grafted back to life, and an estate opened in 2025.
question_meta: Eindhoven's oldest tree is a copper beech in the Glorieuxpark, from a planting band of 1700 to 1750. Where it stands, and fifteen more worth the walk.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Eindhoven is a copper beech in the Glorieuxpark on the Geldropseweg, which the national register of monumental trees places in a planting band of 1700 to 1750, so somewhere between about 275 and 325 years old. It stands on ground that was the Eikenburg estate long before the Brothers of Charity bought it in 1894 and built a boys' boarding school there. The claim has a rival: the Wereldboom foundation puts the plane tree at Groendomein Wasven at around 1760, while the same national register gives that tree a band of 1820 to 1830. Both cannot be right, and neither tree has been cored, so the honest answer is that the beech is the oldest by the register and the plane may be older by its foundation.
question_context: Every age on this page comes from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so ages here are bands and are not narrowed to look precise. That register is the 2024 edition and is a single source for most of these trees, which is why several are flagged. Where a second source exists it is named in the story, and the two trees with the most reporting behind them are the Philips chestnut at the stadium and the plane at Wasven. That plane is the one to watch: it was set on fire in July 2022 and arborists gave it a thirty percent chance of pulling through, so if you walk out there and find it has not made it, tell us and we will take it down the same day. Pins marked approximate mean the park is known and the trunk is not, which matters most at De Wielewaal, where the estate runs to 144 hectares and the oak avenues all look alike.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Eindhoven?
faq.a: A copper beech in the Glorieuxpark, which the national register places in a planting band of 1700 to 1750. The plane tree at Wasven is given around 1760 by the foundation that named it and 1820 to 1830 by the same register, so the two claims overlap and neither tree has been cored.

faq.q: Can you visit Landgoed De Wielewaal?
faq.a: Yes, and only since 27 September 2025. It was Frits Philips's private estate and stayed closed for a century. The city bought it in 2022 for 29 million euro and opened it free of charge, 144 hectares with three entrances at Elburglaan 2, Elburglaan 12 and Oirschotsedijk 3. Mountain bikes and motor vehicles are not allowed.

faq.q: Why are so many of these Philips trees?
faq.a: Because Philips built most of the green in this city. Anton Philips bought the Wielewaal estate in 1912 and 25 hectares of pine wood the same year, gave the second to the people of Eindhoven in 1920, and planted trees in the workers' housing on the theory that staff performed better in green surroundings. The company laid out the parks, so the old trees are standing in them.

All sixteen. The Wielewaal, the Philips de Jongh park and Groendomein Wasven are open public parks with no charge, the Philips chestnut stands on the square outside the stadium, and the Lichtjesboom is a street tree. The Glorieuxpark is owned by a religious order and the register records it as visitable. The Sint Trudo and Antonius churchyards in Strijp are working Catholic cemeteries, open daily and free to walk through. Five more stand outside the Van Abbemuseum, on Pastoor Sickingstraat, in the park behind the Stadspaviljoen, and at Marienhage, all open ground with no charge.

trees.name: The Philips Tree
trees.age_estimate: about 117 years, from a documented planting in 1909

location.address: Frederiklaan 10a, on the square at gate 11 of the Philips Stadium

trees.story:
It has 470 square metres of ground reserved for its roots, in a city centre, next to a football stadium. That is the detail worth knowing: somebody drew a line on a map and decided nothing would ever be built inside it.

Anton Philips had the chestnut planted in 1909 in Philipsdorp, the neighbourhood his company was about to build for its workers. The reasoning was not sentimental. Philips believed staff performed better with something green around them, and the tree went in a year before the first houses did.

So it is older than the district, older than the stadium beside it, and older than the club that plays there, which the company founded in 1913. The houses went up around it, the ground was cleared for the ground, the stands grew, and the chestnut kept its square.

On a match day forty thousand people walk past it and most of them do not look up. Gate 11 is the one to aim for. It is the tree standing in its own patch of open ground while everything else is paving.

Horse chestnuts flower in candles in May and drop conkers in September, which in this spot means several thousand people kicking them across a car park.
trees.access: Free. Public square outside the stadium, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: Eindhoven Centraal, then about 15 minutes on foot west, or bus to Philips Stadion.
trees.how_to_recognise: The only large chestnut on the stadium square, standing in a marked open bed of its own rather than in paving.

best_time.label: May, when the candles are up

trees.name: De Gevlekte Zuiderling
trees.age_estimate: roughly 200 years by the national register, closer to 265 by the foundation that named it

location.address: Groendomein Wasven, Celebeslaan 30, in the old castle park behind the scouting hut

trees.story:
On the night of 28 July 2022 three teenagers set this tree on fire. The brigade put it out, the bark and the base of the trunk were charred through, and arborists put its chances of surviving at thirty percent. What they could not tell was whether the heat had cooked the sap flow, and the answer would not be visible until the spring of 2024.

It came back. Thirty strong shoots pushed up from the ground around the trunk, and rather than clear them a specialist began weaving them together, using an American technique, into a living scaffold that will hold the old trunk up as it rots over the next thirty years. A crowdfunder raised eleven thousand euro. The burnt platform around the base was cut away by hand so the roots were not disturbed.

It stands 28 metres tall with a trunk eight metres round at the base, in the park of a castle that was demolished in 1872. In October 2009 it became the first Wereldboom in the Netherlands.

Its age is disputed. The foundation that named it says planted around 1760; the national register says the 1820s. Nobody has cored it.

Go and look at the black trunk and the young growth climbing it.
trees.access: Free. Public park at Groendomein Wasven, open daily.
trees.transport: About 4 km east of Eindhoven Centraal. Bus to Tongelre, then a short walk into the Wasven grounds.
trees.how_to_recognise: Unmistakable: a huge plane with a blackened, hollowing trunk base and a ring of young shoots trained up around it.

trees.name: The Oak of De Wielewaal
trees.age_estimate: roughly 170 to 180 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860

location.address: Landgoed De Wielewaal, entrances at Elburglaan 2, Elburglaan 12 and Oirschotsedijk 3

trees.story:
For a hundred years you could not come here. This was the private estate of Frits Philips, who built the house in 1934 and lived in it until he died in 2005, on land his father Anton had bought in 1912 when it was a farm called Het Zwarte Huis. The city bought the whole thing in 2022 for twenty nine million euro and opened it to the public on 27 September 2025.

It is 144 hectares, three times the size of the Vondelpark, and entry is free.

This oak was already standing when Anton Philips arrived. In 1850 the ground here was open heath; it was planted up over the second half of the century, and by 1897 the map showed pine wood cut through by avenues of oak. This is one of those avenue trees, which is why it is a good deal older than most of what surrounds it.

The estate is large enough that the pin marks the surveyed position rather than a spot you can stand on and be certain. Come in from Oirschotsedijk and follow the old avenue lines; they are still legible in the way the wood is laid out, and the oaks along them are the thick ones.
trees.access: Free. Public since 27 September 2025. No mountain bikes or motor vehicles.
trees.transport: About 5 km northwest of Eindhoven Centraal. Entrances at Elburglaan 2 and 12 and Oirschotsedijk 3.
trees.how_to_recognise: A heavy old oak standing in a line with others, along one of the straight avenues cut through the pine wood.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down along the avenue

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of the Wielewaal Pinetum
trees.age_estimate: roughly 105 to 115 years, from the register's planting band of 1910 to 1920

location.address: Landgoed De Wielewaal, in the pinetum, entrances at Elburglaan 2, Elburglaan 12 and Oirschotsedijk 3

trees.story:
In 1912 Anton Philips bought a farm on the heath and immediately started collecting conifers. He laid out a pinetum, a star wood with paths radiating from a single point, a maze and a rockery, which tells you what kind of man he was about land: it was to be arranged.

This is one of the trees from that planting, a giant sequoia, a species from the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada that had been in European gardens for about sixty years when it went in here. In California they are the largest living things on earth. In a Brabant pinetum a hundred-year-old one is a tall, red-brown column with bark you can push your fist into, soft and fibrous and thick enough to have evolved against forest fire.

It has a long way to go. Sequoias run to three thousand years and this one is barely out of its first century, which is the pleasant thing about standing under it: on its own timescale, the entire Philips story happened this morning.

The pinetum is signposted from the Oirschotsedijk entrance. Look for the conifer that is obviously wider than everything around it.
trees.transport: About 5 km northwest of Eindhoven Centraal. Nearest entrance Oirschotsedijk 3.
trees.how_to_recognise: The thickest conifer in the pinetum, with deeply furrowed red-brown bark that gives under a push.

trees.name: The Oak by the Wilhelmina Monument
trees.age_estimate: roughly 170 to 180 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860

location.address: Philips de Jonghpark, Bezuidenhoutseweg, left of the path to the Wilhelmina monument

trees.story:
In 1920 Anton Philips and his wife Anna de Jongh gave twenty five hectares of wood to the people of Eindhoven. They had bought it as pine plantation in 1912, turned it into something you could walk in, and handed it over after the neighbouring municipality of Strijp was absorbed into the city. The garden architect D. F. Tersteeg laid it out in the English landscape manner, grass opening into stands of trees, and it opened as a park in 1924.

This oak was there before any of that. The register puts it in the 1850s, which makes it sixty years older than the purchase and a survivor of whatever stood here when the ground was still being planted up from heath.

That is worth holding in mind while you look at it. The park is a designed thing, made by a company for its workers and then given away. The oak is not part of the design. It was simply already standing where somebody later decided to put a path.

It stands to the left of the path running to the Wilhelmina monument. The park was fully renovated in 2009, so the surroundings are tidier than the tree.
trees.access: Free. Public city park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 4 km northwest of Eindhoven Centraal, off the Bezuidenhoutseweg.
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad old oak on the left of the path leading to the Wilhelmina monument, heavier in the trunk than the trees planted around it.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Glorieuxpark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 275 to 325 years, from the register's planting band of 1700 to 1750
trees.story:
This is the oldest thing standing in Eindhoven, by a wide margin and by the register's own dating: a planting band of 1700 to 1750, so somewhere between about 275 and 325 years. Everything else on this page is a Philips tree. This one was full grown before the family arrived.

The ground has changed hands and purpose repeatedly around it. It was the Eikenburg estate; in 1894 the Brothers of Charity bought it and opened a boys' boarding school, adding pavilions over the decades; the boarding school closed in 1996 for lack of pupils, and care and education organisations moved into the buildings. The main house, the old school, the chapel and a mounted statue of Saint George are all listed national monuments. A religious order still owns the park, and the register records it as visitable.

One honest note. This park also held the thickest beech in the whole of North Brabant, and it is gone: a large part of its crown came down on its own in September 2013 and the remaining trunk was taken out. That was a different tree, a green beech, and the register recorded this one eleven years afterwards. If you go and find this one has followed it, tell us.
trees.access: Free. Park owned by a religious order, recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Eindhoven Centraal, on the Geldropseweg.
trees.how_to_recognise: A very heavy beech with dark purple leaves, in the park around the old boarding school buildings.

best_time.label: October, when the purple burns through to copper

trees.name: De Lichtjesboom
trees.age_estimate: roughly 100 to 110 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930

location.address: Diepmeerven 30 to 32, in the planting strip along the street

trees.story:
Every December the neighbourhood covers this oak in fairy lights, and keeps them on through January. It is not a municipal display and nobody is paid to do it. That is why the street knows it as the lichtjesboom, the little lights tree, rather than by anything the register calls it.

The rest of the year it is a good ordinary oak of about a century, standing clear of the houses in the strip of planting along the Diepmeerven, well enough placed that you see the whole shape of it from the pavement. The street name probably points at the Diepe Meerven, a small heath pool a way off toward Heeze, which is what this whole district was before it was a district.

It is the smallest tree on this page and the only one on it because of what people do with it. Eindhoven is a city that thinks about light more than most, having spent a century making it, and the version that matters here is a hundred bulbs strung through an oak by people who live on the street.

Go in December. In August you will see an oak.
trees.access: Free. Street tree in a public planting strip.
trees.transport: About 5 km southeast of Eindhoven Centraal, in the Gijzenrooi district.
trees.how_to_recognise: The one free-standing oak in the green strip along the Diepmeerven, opposite numbers 30 to 32. In winter it is the one with the lights.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Copper Beech of Sint Trudo Churchyard

location.address: Strijpsestraat 127, churchyard behind the Sint Trudokerk, Strijp, Eindhoven

trees.story:
Strijp was its own village until 1919, and this copper beech is older than the annexation that folded it into Eindhoven. It stands in the churchyard of the Sint Trudokerk, part of a monumental avenue of beeches that lines the entrance on both sides, graves running in rows beneath them toward a small hill topped with a cross.

The church itself has had a rough run for a building not yet a century and a half old: consecrated in 1887, damaged by fire in 1936, rebuilt with a new tower over 1937 and 1938, then bomb damaged again in 1944, with repairs not finished until 1949. The beech avenue beside it, planted in the 1890s, predates every one of those disasters and outlasted them all.

The tree register lists three more copper beeches within a stone's throw, close enough together that they read as one avenue rather than four separate specimens worth visiting on their own. This is the one the register singles out by coordinate, multi-stemmed and roughly 130 years old, in an ordinary Catholic churchyard that has quietly kept growing through a century its own parish church did not get to enjoy.
trees.access: Free. Public Catholic churchyard behind the Sint-Trudokerk in Strijp, open daily.
trees.transport: Eindhoven Strijp-S railway station, about 12-15 minutes' walk, or bus lines serving Strijpsestraat.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1694310) designates this copper beech, multi-stemmed, planted band 1890-1900. gedenk-cultuur.nl independently confirms a monumental beech entrance avenue at the same churchyard (general match, not this specific specimen by coordinate, hence flagged). Three further register 'Bruine beuk' entries sit within 100-150m in the same avenue, treated as one collectible ensemble per the register-twins rule rather than shipped separately. No girth recorded (LRMB carries no girth field).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the multi-stemmed copper beech the register singles out among four standing in the same avenue. It stands in the churchyard behind the Sint Trudokerk, Strijp.

trees.name: The Box Elder of Antonius Kerkhof
trees.story:
This box elder outlived the parish that planted it. The Antonius kerkhof belonged to a Eindhoven congregation nicknamed the Steentjeskerk, split off from the older Trudo parish in 1919 and folded back into it in 1977 when it could no longer stand alone. The tree, planted sometime in the 1920s, has stood through the whole rise and fall.

The national tree register flags it for two reasons at once, rare for this kind of entry: real aesthetic value, and a species genuinely uncommon in this part of the country. Box elder is an ordinary enough tree across much of North America, but a century old specimen singled out by an official Dutch register is a different thing, and this small, half forgotten churchyard is where it happens to be growing.

The cemetery itself closed to new burials in 2007, taking only urns since, which is usually how a place like this drifts toward being quietly overlooked. It has not been: it still opens daily from ten to five, still belongs to an active parish, and this tree is one of several worth the walk inside its low walls.
trees.access: Free. Small Catholic churchyard (about 0.85 ha), open daily 10:00-17:00.
trees.transport: About 1.3 km from Eindhoven city centre; several bus lines stop nearby on Kronehoefstraat/Fransebaan.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1697130) designates one Box Elder, single stem, planted band 1920-1930, flagged by the register itself for high aesthetic value and regional rarity. Only the register and a general cemetery-access source were found, so flagged per the one-source rule.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a box elder, an uncommon species here for its age, growing inside the churchyard's low walls. It stands at Doelenstraat 2, Antonius kerkhof.

trees.name: The Nordmann Firs of Antonius Kerkhof
trees.story:
The world's most popular Christmas tree does not usually get old enough to become a monument. Nordmann fir is grown by the millions and cut down each December long before it can reach any real age, so a stand of three growing undisturbed in the Antonius kerkhof for roughly a century is exactly the kind of anomaly a tree register exists to flag.

Planted in the 1920s in this small Catholic churchyard, once the burial ground of a parish nicknamed the Steentjeskerk before it merged back into the older Trudo parish in 1977, the three firs stand together as one dark, upright stand rather than as separate trees to find one by one. Nobody appears to have written about them beyond the register that designates them, which is unsurprising: a conifer doing exactly what a conifer does, only for a hundred years instead of one winter, is a quiet kind of remarkable.

They stand a few dozen metres from the churchyard's box elder and its oak by the gate, close enough to see all three on one short visit. The churchyard opens daily, ten to five, free, no ticket, evergreen whatever the season.
trees.access: Free. Small Catholic churchyard (about 0.85 ha), open daily 10:00-17:00.
trees.transport: About 1.3 km from Eindhoven city centre; several bus lines stop nearby on Kronehoefstraat/Fransebaan.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1695680) designates a group of three Nordmann firs at one coordinate, planted band 1920-1930, reason 'monumentaal'. Treated as one collectible entry per the register-twins/ensemble rule. Only the register and a general cemetery-access source were found, so flagged per the one-source rule.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as three Nordmann firs standing together as one dark, upright stand, a few dozen metres from the churchyard's box elder. They stand at Doelenstraat 2, Antonius kerkhof.

trees.name: The Oak at the Gate of Antonius Kerkhof

location.address: Doelenstraat 2, Antonius kerkhof, Eindhoven (just inside the entrance, right of the caretaker's house)

trees.story:
This oak is the first tree anyone meets walking into the Antonius kerkhof, standing just inside the gate beside the old caretaker's house. It was only recently added to the national tree register, which is a different thing from being recently planted: it has stood here since sometime in the 1920s, a full century, and simply went unrecorded until somebody finally looked.

The churchyard it guards belonged to a parish nicknamed the Steentjeskerk, briefly independent from the older Trudo parish from 1919 until the two merged back together in 1977. Burials stopped here in 2007, urns only since, but the gate still opens daily and the oak still does the job an entrance tree does anywhere: mark the threshold, offer shade to whoever pauses before going further in.

Further in stand a box elder and a group of three Nordmann firs, both also drawn from the same register and both worth the same short walk. None of the three has much written about it beyond the register that designates it, which is the honest state of a small churchyard nobody has thought to study closely, only to protect.
trees.access: Free. Small Catholic churchyard (about 0.85 ha), open daily 10:00-17:00.
trees.transport: About 1.3 km from Eindhoven city centre; several bus lines stop nearby on Kronehoefstraat/Fransebaan.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1695439) designates one Pedunculate Oak just inside the churchyard entrance, planted band 1920-1930, reason 'nieuw' (recently added to the register). Only the register and a general cemetery-access source were found, so flagged per the one-source rule.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the first tree inside the gate, standing beside the old caretaker's house. It stands in the Antonius kerkhof, Doelenstraat 2, Eindhoven.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Catalpa of the Van Abbemuseum
trees.age_estimate: around a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.neighbourhood: Eindhoven city centre, on the Dommel beside the Van Abbemuseum

trees.access: Free. Public green strip (plantsoen) beside the museum's main entrance, open at all times.
trees.transport: Eindhoven Centraal, about 15 minutes on foot south along the Dommel, or bus to the Van Abbemuseum stop.
trees.story:
Nobody can say whether this catalpa or the museum beside it came first. The national tree register puts its planting between 1900 and 1910. Eindhoven's own tree database, refreshed this month, records 1930. Both are official, both list the tree as monumental, and the gap between them is a generation. It matters here, because the Van Abbemuseum went up in 1936, built by A.J. Kropholler for the cigar manufacturer Henri van Abbe to hold his collection. On the register's dating the tree was already thirty years old and watched the building arrive on its doorstep. On the city's dating it went in six years before the builders did. We have not picked a winner between the two.

What is not in dispute: this is a southern catalpa of fifteen to eighteen metres, on the public green strip between the museum and the Dommel, and it is not alone. Four more catalpas stand within thirty five metres, all of them carrying the same monumental rating in the city's records. Catalpa comes from the southeastern United States, and it keeps American hours: it is one of the last trees in a Dutch park to come into leaf, so in April this corner still looks bare while everything around it has gone green. By July the crown is full of white flowers marked in yellow and purple.

If you know when these were planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad heart-shaped leaves, which appear weeks later than anything around them, and by its height of fifteen to eighteen metres. It stands on the green strip between the Van Abbemuseum and the Dommel.

best_time.label: July, when the white flowers open across the crown

trees.name: The Cedar of Pastoor Sickingstraat
trees.access: Free. Stands in a paved urban street setting, visible from the public street at all times.
trees.transport: About 1.7 km southeast of Eindhoven Centraal (Joriskwartier, Stratum); bus lines serve nearby Aalsterweg, or about 20 minutes on foot.
trees.story:
Eindhoven's own tree database contradicts itself about this tree. One field of the record calls it a blue Atlas cedar. Another field in the same record gives the species as Cedrus libani, the cedar of Lebanon, which is what the national register calls it as well. The two registers point at the same spot, less than three metres apart, so this is one tree wearing two labels rather than two trees. The species are close relatives and genuinely hard to tell apart: both hold their branches out flat in layers, both carry short needles in tufts, and it is the cones and the needle detail that settle the question. We have listed it as the cedar of Lebanon because two of the three entries say so, and we are flagging the disagreement rather than tidying it away. If you can settle it standing underneath, tell us.

The rest is plainer. The city dates the planting to 1930, which puts the tree at about ninety-five years, and records it at fifteen to eighteen metres. The national register lists its history as unknown, which is a register's way of saying nobody ever wrote anything down about it.

Its surroundings are far younger than it is. The Joriskwartier went up mostly around 2006, by which time this cedar had been standing for some seventy-five years. It now holds a layered evergreen crown over a paved street, in a neighbourhood built around it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the branches held out flat in layers and the short blue-green needles in tufts, a cedar of fifteen to eighteen metres. It stands on the Pastoor Sickingstraat, in paving rather than grass.

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.name: The Honey Locust of the Stadspaviljoen
trees.age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.address: Alberdingk Thijmlaan 1, Stadswandelpark, behind the Stadspaviljoen, Eindhoven

trees.transport: About 1.3 km south of Eindhoven Centraal, inside the Stadswandelpark; several bus lines serve the park's edges, or about 15-20 minutes on foot.
trees.story:
This honey locust stands more than twenty-four metres tall, which the species almost never manages in the Netherlands. Gleditsia triacanthos is an American tree from the Mississippi basin, planted in European cities for its fine feathery leaflets and its indifference to bad air, and it usually stops well short of that height here. Eindhoven's tree survey files this one in its top band, above twenty-four metres. The national register lists it on dendrological grounds, which is a register saying the tree earns its protection for what it is rather than for anything that happened to it.

Its age is disputed. The register bands the planting between 1890 and 1900, which would make it about 130 years old. The city's record says 1940, which would make it 86. Nobody has reconciled the two and we are not going to pick one for them.

It stands behind the Stadspaviljoen, once the coach house of Landgoed Den Elzent. The tobacco manufacturer H.F.C. Coolen sold that estate in 1876 to the Amsterdam merchant B.H.A. Sinkel, who had Leonard Springer lay the grounds out as a landscape garden. Eindhoven opened them to the public in 1921 and named the place Stadswandelpark ten years later. The corner is a group rather than a single specimen: beeches, pin oaks, black locusts and a sweet chestnut a few steps away, all of them monumental in the city's records.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fine feathery leaflets, small for a tree of its size, and by its height of over twenty-four metres. It stands behind the Stadspaviljoen in the Stadswandelpark, near a sweet chestnut.

best_time.label: October, when the small leaflets turn clear yellow and come down early

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of the Stadspaviljoen
trees.age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.address: Alberdingk Thijmlaan, Stadswandelpark, behind the Stadspaviljoen, Eindhoven

trees.transport: About 1.3 km south of Eindhoven Centraal, inside the Stadswandelpark; several bus lines serve the park's edges, or about 15-20 minutes on foot.
trees.story:
Two registers place this chestnut within eighty centimetres of each other and disagree about its age by fifty years. The national register bands the planting 1890 to 1900. Eindhoven's own tree database says 1940. The position is settled and the age is not, which is the usual shape of these things: somebody once stood under the tree with a GPS, and nobody ever counted anything.

The species is not in dispute. A sweet chestnut in a Dutch park is a food tree that stopped being used as one. Castanea sativa came north with the Romans, who ground the nuts into flour, and it fed people across southern Europe for centuries afterwards. This one reaches fifteen to eighteen metres, hangs cream catkins in July, and in October drops spiny burrs into the grass, where the squirrels reach them first.

It stands behind the Stadspaviljoen, a few dozen metres from the honey locust, which makes the pair one short walk rather than two separate errands. The pavilion was the coach house of Landgoed Den Elzent, a private country estate on the edge of town until Eindhoven opened the grounds to the public in 1921. The trees in this corner are a set rather than a scatter: beeches, pin oaks and black locusts, all of them monumental in the city's records, dated by the city to 1910 and 1940.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long leaves with saw-toothed edges and, in autumn, by the spiny husks lying in the grass under it. It stands behind the Stadspaviljoen, a few dozen metres from the much taller honey locust.

best_time.label: October, when the spiny burrs split and the chestnuts come down

trees.name: The Plane of Marienhage
trees.age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.address: Kanaalstraat 6, behind the former Marienhage monastery, Eindhoven
location.neighbourhood: Eindhoven city centre, on the Dommel

trees.access: Free; the LRMB register lists it as visitable, but it is not visible from the street. It stands behind the former Marienhage monastery (now a hotel, DomusDELA/Hotel Marienhage) against the Dommel; reach it via the public Dommelpad riverside walking route, which is documented as passing this exact site (Marienhage is a marked stage point of the long-distance 'Ons Kloosterpad' trail).
trees.transport: Eindhoven Centraal, about 10 minutes on foot, near Kanaalstraat / the Dommel.
trees.story:
This plane stands more than twenty-four metres tall and you cannot see it from the street. It grows behind Marienhage on the bank of the Dommel, screened by the buildings, and the national register says as much in its own fields: reachable, but not visible from the road.

There has been a religious house on this ground since 1419, when Augustinian hermits founded a cloister on the river outside what was then a small town. The complex was rebuilt in the last quarter of the nineteenth century, ran as a monastery and a school for generations, and was sold in 2017. It is a hotel and a cultural venue now, which is a strange fate for a cloister and a fortunate one for the tree, since the garden came with it.

How old the plane is depends on which register you ask. The national one bands the planting between 1880 and 1890, which would make it about 140. Eindhoven's own tree database says 1935, which makes it 91. Neither source explains the other and we have not picked a side.

Getting to it asks a little faith in the map. Public footpaths run through the riverside grounds, the site's redevelopment plan undertook to open the garden, and Marienhage is a marked stop on the Dommelpad walking route. None of that proves the path takes you within sight of this particular tree, so go expecting a short hunt along the water.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flaking, patchy plane bark and a crown of over twenty-four metres. It stands on the bank of the Dommel behind the old Marienhage monastery, out of sight of Kanaalstraat.
